A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Complexification and conjugation.** Complex scalars act by
$c(h\otimes z)=h\otimes cz$; this respects the rational balancing relations.
A finite rational basis of $H$ identifies $H_{\mathbb C}$ with the corresponding
finite-dimensional coordinate space over $\mathbb C$. The
$\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

**Tensor and dual conventions.** The tensor product $H\otimes K$ carries
$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the weight sum is taken over $\mathbb Q$ and the Hodge sum over
$\mathbb C$, using $(H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}K)_{\mathbb C}\cong
H_{\mathbb C}\otimes_{\mathbb C}K_{\mathbb C}$; the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

For an increasing filtration, the **associated graded object** is the indexed family
$$\operatorname{gr}^F_pA=\operatorname{coker}(F_{p-1}A\hookrightarrow F_pA)=F_pA/F_{p-1}A\quad(p\in\mathbb Z).$$
For a decreasing filtration it is $\operatorname{gr}^p_FA=F^pA/F^{p+1}A$. Here the inclusions come from [[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]], and quotient means [[def-the-quotient-of-an-object-by-a-subobject]]. This definition uses a family; it assumes no infinite direct sum. With $F^p=F_{-p}$, the decreasing piece at $p$ is the increasing piece at $-p$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $U$ be a finite family of linear subspaces $U_i$ of
$V$ indexed by $i < n$ ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]); as everywhere on this page the index runs over
the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]).

**The sum of the other summands.** The set $\{0_V\}$ is a linear subspace of $V$:
it contains $0_V$, it is closed under addition since $0_V + 0_V = 0_V$, and it is
closed under scalar multiplication since $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]). So for each $j < n$ the family
$U^{(j)}$ defined by

$$U^{(j)}_i := U_i \quad (i \ne j), \qquad U^{(j)}_j := \{0_V\}$$

is again a finite family of linear subspaces of $V$ indexed by $i < n$, and we
write

$$\sum_{i \ne j} U_i \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} U^{(j)}_i ,$$

a linear subspace of $V$ by [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]. Replacing the
$j$-th summand by $\{0_V\}$, rather than re-indexing over a smaller set, keeps
every family on this page indexed by a natural number.

**The definition.** $V$ is the **internal direct sum** of the family $U$, written

$$V \;=\; \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i ,$$

when both of the following hold:

- **(D1)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i<n} U_i = V$;
- **(D2)** for every $j < n$,
  $\displaystyle U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$.

In (D2) the inclusion $\supseteq$ is automatic, since $U_j$ and
$\sum_{i \ne j} U_i$ are linear subspaces and each therefore contains $0_V$; the
content of (D2) is the inclusion $\subseteq$, that no nonzero vector of $U_j$ is
a sum of vectors drawn from the other summands.

### Two summands

Take $n = 2$ and write $U := U_0$, $W := U_1$. For $j = 0$ the family $U^{(0)}$ is
$\{0_V\}, W$, so $\sum_{i \ne 0} U_i = \{\, 0_V + w : w \in W \,\} = W$; for
$j = 1$ it is $U$ in the same way. So (D2) reduces to the single condition
$U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and

$$V = U \oplus W \quad\text{means}\quad U + W = V \ \text{ and } \ U \cap W = \{0_V\}.$$

For two summands, therefore, (D2) and the pairwise condition coincide; this is
the familiar form of the definition.

### Three or more summands: (D2) is not the pairwise condition

For $n \ge 3$ the condition (D2) is **strictly stronger** than requiring
$U_i \cap U_j = \{0_V\}$ for all $i \ne j$.

That (D2) implies the pairwise condition is immediate: for $i \ne j$ with
$i, j < n$ we have $U_i = U^{(j)}_i \subseteq \sum_{i \ne j} U_i$, since a sum of
a family contains each of its summands ([[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]]), so
$U_j \cap U_i \subseteq U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$, and the reverse
inclusion holds because both are linear subspaces.

The converse fails, and it fails already for three summands: a family can satisfy
(D1) and have all its pairwise intersections trivial while (D2) is false, so that
decompositions are not unique. The companion examples page records a witness. A
definition stated with the pairwise condition in place of (D2) would therefore be
a different, and weaker, notion, and the characterisation by unique decomposition
([[lem-direct-sum-criterion]]) would be false for it.

### The empty family

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so $n = 0$ is a genuine case. Then
$\sum_{i<0} U_i = \{0_V\}$ ([[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]) and (D2) is vacuous,
there being no $j < 0$. So $V = \bigoplus_{i<0} U_i$ holds exactly when
$V = \{0_V\}$: the zero space is the direct sum of the empty family, and no other
space is.

derivations.claim: (Two-filtration lemma, spanning and partial sums.) Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$ such that $V=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV)$ for an integer $n$. Then (i) $F^aV+\bar F^{n+1-a}V=V$ for every $a$, and (ii) $F^aV=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, with the conjugate formula $\bar F^bV=\bigoplus_{q\ge b}(F^{n-q}V\cap\bar F^qV)$. For (i), write $v=\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q}$; the terms with $p\ge a$ sum into $F^aV$, and each remaining term has $p<a$, hence $q=n-p>n-a$, that is $q\ge n+1-a$, so their sum lies in $\bar F^{n+1-a}V$. For (ii), prove $F^aV\subseteq\sum_{p\ge a}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$ by descending induction on $a$: the claim is trivial when $F^aV=0$, and otherwise (i) with $a+1$ gives $V=F^{a+1}V+\bar F^{n-a}V$, so the modular law applied to $F^{a+1}V\subseteq F^aV\subseteq V$ yields $F^aV=F^{a+1}V+(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$, in which the induction hypothesis places $F^{a+1}V$ inside $\sum_{p\ge a+1}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$ while $F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V$ is the term with $p=a$; the reverse inclusion is clear, and the sum is direct because the pieces $F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V$ are independent by the decomposition hypothesis, which is symmetric in the two filtrations, so the same argument with $F$ and $\bar F$ interchanged gives the formula for $\bar F^bV$.

(Two-filtration lemma, vanishing.) Under the hypothesis of step 1.1, $F^aV\cap\bar F^bV=0$ whenever $a+b>n$. Indeed, let $x\in F^aV\cap\bar F^bV$ and let $x=\sum_{p+q=n}x_{p,q}$ be its unique decomposition with $x_{p,q}\in F^pV\cap\bar F^qV$. Since $x\in F^aV$, its decomposition lies in $\bigoplus_{p\ge a}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$ by step 1.1 (ii), so $x_{p,n-p}=0$ for every $p<a$; since $x\in\bar F^bV$, the conjugate half of step 1.1 (ii) gives $x_{n-q,q}=0$ for every $q<b$. If $x\ne0$, some $x_{p,n-p}$ is nonzero, and it satisfies $p\ge a$ and $n-p\ge b$, whence $n=p+(n-p)\ge a+b>n$, a contradiction; so $x=0$.

(Lifting.) Let $m=p+q$. Every $d\in W_{m-1}$ can be written as $d=z+g$ with $z\in F^p\cap W_{m-1}$ and $g\in(\bar F^q\cap W_{m-1})+\sum_{j\ge1}(\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1})$. To see this, construct elements $d_1,d_2,\dots$ and vectors $f_j,g_j$ as follows. Put $d_1=d$, and suppose $d_j\in W_{m-j}$ has been constructed for some $j\ge1$. By [F1] the induced filtrations on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-j}$ are $(m-j)$-opposed, and step 1.1 (i) applied there with the pair $(p,q-j+1)$, whose indices sum to $m-j+1$, shows that the images of $F^p\cap W_{m-j}$ and $\bar F^{q-j+1}\cap W_{m-j}$ generate $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-j}$; choose $f_j\in F^p\cap W_{m-j}$ and $g_j\in\bar F^{q-j+1}\cap W_{m-j}$ whose classes sum to the class of $d_j$, and put $d_{j+1}:=d_j-f_j-g_j\in W_{m-j-1}$. By [F2] there is $J$ with $W_{m-J}=0$; the recursion stops there, and summing the identities $d_{j+1}=d_j-f_j-g_j$ gives $d=\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(f_j+g_j)$. Each $f_j$ lies in $F^p\cap W_{m-j}\subseteq F^p\cap W_{m-1}$; $g_1$ lies in $\bar F^q\cap W_{m-1}$ and, for $j\ge2$, $g_j$ lies in $\bar F^{q-(j-1)}\cap W_{m-(j-1)-1}$. Hence $z:=\sum_jf_j$ and $g:=\sum_jg_j$ have the required properties.

(Surjectivity onto the graded summand.) Let $\xi\in H^{p,q}_m$. Since $H^{p,q}_m\subseteq F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ is the image of $F^p\cap W_m$, choose $x_0\in F^p\cap W_m$ representing $\xi$; since $H^{p,q}_m\subseteq\bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ is the image of $\bar F^q\cap W_m$, choose $y_0\in\bar F^q\cap W_m$ also representing $\xi$. Then $d:=x_0-y_0$ lies in $W_{m-1}$, so step 2.2 gives $d=z+g$ with $z\in F^p\cap W_{m-1}$ and $g$ in the displayed sum. Put $x:=x_0-z=y_0+g$. Then $x\in F^p\cap W_m$, and $x\in(\bar F^q\cap W_m)+\sum_{j\ge1}(\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1})$ because $y_0$ lies in the first summand and $g$ in the sum; so $x\in I^{p,q}$. Finally $x-x_0=-z\in W_{m-1}$, so $x$ and $x_0$ have the same class $\xi$ in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$. Hence the projection maps $I^{p,q}$ onto $H^{p,q}_m$, and $I^{p,q}\subseteq W_m\cap F^p$ holds by definition.

(Injectivity modulo the lower weight.) Suppose $0\ne x\in I^{p,q}\cap W_{m-1}$, and choose its least weight index $r$, so $x\in W_r\setminus W_{r-1}$ and $r<m$. Write $x=y+\sum_{j\ge1}g_j$ as in the defining formula, with $y\in\bar F^q\cap W_m$ and $g_j\in\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1}$; only finitely many terms are needed because $W$ is finite. Put $J=m-r-1\ge0$. The sum $\sum_{j>J}g_j$ lies in $W_{r-1}$, while $h:=y+\sum_{1\le j\le J}g_j$ lies in $\bar F^{q-J}$ and also in $W_r$, because $h=x-\sum_{j>J}g_j$. Thus the nonzero class of $x$ in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_r$ belongs to $F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_r\cap\bar F^{q-J}\operatorname{Gr}^W_r$. But $p+q-J=r+1>r$, so step 2.1 makes that intersection zero, a contradiction. Together with step 3.1 this proves the projection isomorphism in (a).

(The weight decomposition and the direct-sum identity.) For every $m$ the projection restricts to an isomorphism $\bigoplus_{p+q=m}I^{p,q}\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH_{\mathbb C}$: by steps 3.1 and 4.1 each $I^{p,q}$ maps isomorphically onto $H^{p,q}_m$, and by [F1] the summands $H^{p,q}_m$ are independent with sum $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$. In particular $\dim I^{p,q}=\dim H^{p,q}_m$, so $\sum_{p+q=m}\dim I^{p,q}=\dim\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ for every $m$. The sum map $\psi_m\colon\bigoplus_{p+q\le m}I^{p,q}\to W_m$ is injective: if a finite sum $\sum_{m'\le m}\sum_{p+q=m'}x_{p,q}$ vanishes, its class in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ is the sum of the classes of the top pieces $x_{p,m-p}$, which vanishes only if each of those pieces is zero because the restricted projection is an isomorphism; subtracting them leaves a vanishing sum over $m'\le m-1$, and induction on $m$ (with $W_m=0$ for all sufficiently negative $m$) finishes the argument. Its image therefore has dimension $\sum_{m'\le m}\dim\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m'}=\dim W_m$, the finite telescoping identity for the finite filtration $W$; an injective map between spaces of equal dimension is an isomorphism, so $W_mH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q\le m}I^{p,q}$. Taking $m$ large gives $H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p,q}I^{p,q}$.

(Conjugation modulo lower weights.) Work in $U=W_m/W_{m-2}$ with the images of $F^p\cap W_m$ and $\bar F^q\cap W_m$. Their intersection $T$ maps injectively to $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$: its intersection with $W_{m-1}/W_{m-2}$ is $F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-1}\cap\bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-1}=0$ by step 2.1, since $p+q=m>m-1$. The formula for $I^{p,q}$ shows its image in $U$ lies in $T$, since every tail term has weight at most $m-2$. Step 3.1 shows this image maps onto $H^{p,q}_m$; the image of $T$ also lies in $H^{p,q}_m$, so injectivity makes the image of $I^{p,q}$ exactly $T$. Conjugating the same argument for $I^{q,p}$ shows that $\sigma(I^{q,p})$ has this same image $T$ in $U$. Therefore $I^{p,q}+W_{m-2}=\sigma(I^{q,p})+W_{m-2}$.

(The Hodge decomposition.) For all $a,m$ one has $F^a\cap W_m=\bigoplus_{p\ge a,\ p+q\le m}I^{p,q}$. Indeed, decompose $x\in F^a\cap W_m$ by step 5.1. Its class in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ lies in $\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,m-p}_m$ by step 1.1, so its top components with $p<a$ vanish by the projection isomorphism. Subtracting the remaining top components leaves an element of $F^a\cap W_{m-1}$, and induction through the finite $W$ proves the assertion. Taking $m$ large proves $F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}I^{p,q}$. Conjugating this identity gives $\bar F^b=\bigoplus_{q\ge b}\sigma(I^{q,p})$; it does not assert a decomposition of $\bar F$ by the original $I^{p,q}$.

(Functoriality.) Let $f\colon H\to K$ be a morphism of rational mixed Hodge structures. Since $f$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$, $f_{\mathbb C}$ commutes with the conjugations, so $f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^qH_{\mathbb C})=\overline{f_{\mathbb C}(F^qH_{\mathbb C})}\subseteq\bar F^qK_{\mathbb C}$; it also satisfies $f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ and $f_{\mathbb C}(W_aH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq W_aK_{\mathbb C}$ by definition. Applying $f_{\mathbb C}$ to the two intersections and the sum defining $I^{p,q}(H)$ therefore produces an element of the corresponding intersection of $F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ with the sum of the $\bar F$-terms for $K$, and $W$-membership is preserved term by term; hence $f_{\mathbb C}(I^{p,q}(H))\subseteq I^{p,q}(K)$.

Let $(H,W,F)$ be a rational mixed Hodge structure
([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]) with complex conjugation $\sigma$ on
$H_{\mathbb C}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, and write
$\bar F^a=\sigma(F^a)$ for the conjugate Hodge filtration; all weight spaces
below are the complexifications $W_aH_{\mathbb C}$. For integers $p,q$ put
$m=p+q$ and
$$I^{p,q}=\bigl(F^p\cap W_m\bigr)\cap\Bigl(\bigl(\bar F^q\cap W_m\bigr)+\sum_{j\ge1}\bigl(\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1}\bigr)\Bigr),$$
the intersections and the sum taken in $H_{\mathbb C}$. Then:

(a) $I^{p,q}\subseteq W_m\cap F^p$, the intersection $I^{p,q}\cap W_{m-1}$ is
zero, and the projection $W_m\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH_{\mathbb C}$ maps
$I^{p,q}$ isomorphically onto the summand $H^{p,q}_m$ of the mixed Hodge
definition;

(b) $W_mH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q\le m}I^{p,q}$,
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}I^{p,q}$ for all integers $a,m$; in
particular $H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p,q}I^{p,q}$;

(c) every morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
satisfies $f_{\mathbb C}(I^{p,q}(H))\subseteq I^{p,q}(K)$.

The construction satisfies
$I^{p,q}+W_{m-2}=\sigma(I^{q,p})+W_{m-2}$ inside $W_m$.
It need not satisfy $\sigma(I^{p,q})=I^{q,p}$, and the same splitting need
not split $\bar F$: its conjugate gives
$\bar F^bH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{q\ge b}\sigma(I^{q,p})$. The splitting is
the one pinned down in the sources by the displayed formula, not an arbitrary
direct-sum decomposition.

A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Complexification and conjugation.** Complex scalars act by
$c(h\otimes z)=h\otimes cz$; this respects the rational balancing relations.
A finite rational basis of $H$ identifies $H_{\mathbb C}$ with the corresponding
finite-dimensional coordinate space over $\mathbb C$. The
$\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

**Tensor and dual conventions.** The tensor product $H\otimes K$ carries
$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the weight sum is taken over $\mathbb Q$ and the Hodge sum over
$\mathbb C$, using $(H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}K)_{\mathbb C}\cong
H_{\mathbb C}\otimes_{\mathbb C}K_{\mathbb C}$; the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

derivations.claim: (Weight strictness.) Let $y=f(x)\in f(H)\cap W_nK$ and decompose $x=\sum_{p,q}x^{p,q}$ along the splitting of $H_{\mathbb C}$; then $y=\sum_{p,q}f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})$ with $f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})\in I^{p,q}(K)$ by [F1]. Since $y\in W_nK=\bigoplus_{p+q\le n}I^{p,q}(K)$ and the sum is direct, all components with $p+q>n$ vanish: $f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})=0$ whenever $p+q>n$. Hence $x':=\sum_{p+q\le n}x^{p,q}$ lies in $W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ and satisfies $f_{\mathbb C}(x')=y$, so $y\in f_{\mathbb C}(W_nH_{\mathbb C})$. The reverse inclusion $f(W_nH)\subseteq f(H)\cap W_nK$ is the preservation of $W$ by $f$.

(Hodge strictness.) The same computation with the condition $p<a$ instead of $p+q>n$: if $y=f_{\mathbb C}(x)\in f(H_{\mathbb C})\cap F^aK_{\mathbb C}$, decompose $x$ and use $F^aK_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}I^{p,q}(K)$ to conclude that $f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})=0$ for $p<a$, so $x'=\sum_{p\ge a}x^{p,q}$ lies in $F^aH_{\mathbb C}$ and maps to $y$.

(Rational descent.) Step 1.1 gives equality of the complexifications of the rational subspaces $A=f(W_nH)$ and $B=f(H)\cap W_nK$. Images and intersections commute with extension from $\mathbb Q$ to $\mathbb C$: in finite rational coordinates they are kernels or images of matrices, whose rank is unchanged on extension since the same nonzero rational minors remain nonzero. To descend $A_{\mathbb C}=B_{\mathbb C}$, map $A$ into the rational quotient $K/B$. Its complexification is zero, hence the rational map is zero (a nonzero rational coordinate remains nonzero over $\mathbb C$), so $A\subseteq B$; interchanging them gives equality. Together with step 1.2 this proves the stated rational $W$ strictness and complex $F$ strictness. Complex conjugation fixes the real scalar extension of a rational space and is not used to recover rational vectors.

(Exactness of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n$.) Let $0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of mixed Hodge structures. By [F1] the splitting identifies $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nA$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nB$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nC$ with $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}I^{p,q}(A)$ and its analogues, and the maps $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n i$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n p$ with the direct sums of the maps induced by $i$ and $p$ between the pieces $I^{p,q}$. Each piecewise sequence $0\to I^{p,q}(A)\to I^{p,q}(B)\to I^{p,q}(C)\to 0$ is exact: injectivity follows by restriction of $i$; to lift $c\in I^{p,q}(C)$, choose a preimage in $B_{\mathbb C}$ and decompose it, whose $(p,q)$ component maps to $c$ by functoriality and uniqueness of the target decomposition. An element $b\in I^{p,q}(B)$ lies in $\ker p$ precisely when $b=i(a)$ for some $a\in A$, and decomposing $a$ into its $I$-pieces shows that all other pieces map to zero; since $i$ is injective, they vanish and $a\in I^{p,q}(A)$. A direct sum of short exact sequences is short exact, so $0\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_nA\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_nB\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_nC\to0$ is exact after complexification. The rational graded sequence is exact as well, since kernels and images commute with scalar extension and rational ranks descend as in step 2.1.

(Kernel, image and cokernel.) The functorial splitting [F1] makes $f_{\mathbb C}$ a direct sum of maps $I^{p,q}(H)\to I^{p,q}(K)$. Thus its kernel, image and cokernel decompose into the respective kernels, images and cokernels of these maps, and their induced or quotient $W$ and $F$ are the partial sums by $p+q\le n$ and $p\ge a$. The projection isomorphisms in [F1] identify their weight-$n$ pieces, with these induced $F$ filtrations, with the kernel, image and cokernel of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n f$, computed componentwise in the pure decompositions $H^{p,q}_n,K^{p,q}_n$. These identifications are the canonical rational graded maps: for a kernel this follows from $W$ strictness, since if $f(x)\in W_{n-1}K$ with $x\in W_nH$, choose $y\in W_{n-1}H$ with $f(y)=f(x)$ and replace $x$ by $x-y$; the image and cokernel follow by the same induced/quotient description. The graded rational map commutes with conjugation and preserves $F$, hence also $\bar F$; between equal-weight pure structures it preserves each type $F^p\cap\bar F^q$ with $p+q=n$. Consequently its pure kernels, images and cokernels have conjugation exchanging their $(p,q)$ and $(q,p)$ pieces. Their $F$ partial sums and their conjugates are therefore $n$-opposed. Every weight-graded piece of the three rational filtered spaces satisfies the mixed Hodge axiom, proving the claim. This argument requires no exact conjugate decomposition on the mixed vector space.

(Pure image.) Now suppose $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nK=K$. By step 3.2 the image is a mixed Hodge structure with the induced filtration, and step 1.1 gives $W_{n-1}(\operatorname{im}f)=f(W_{n-1}H)=0$ and $W_n(\operatorname{im}f)=f(H)\cap W_nK=f(H)=\operatorname{im}f$; hence the image is pure of weight $n$.

Let K be a cochain complex with decreasing filtration by subcomplexes. Set $C_n=K^{-n}$, $F_pC_n=F^{-p}K^{-n}$ and $d_n=d_K^{-n}$. Then
$$E_r^{p,q}(K)=E^r_{-p,-q}(C),\qquad d_r:E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}.$$
The construction gives $E_0^{p,q}=\operatorname{gr}^p K^{p+q}$ and $E_1^{p,q}\cong H^{p+q}(\operatorname{gr}^p K)$. With degreewise finite filtration it naturally abuts to the decreasing image filtration on $H^{p+q}(K)$, with $E_\infty^{p,q}\cong\operatorname{gr}^pH^{p+q}(K)$.

Every morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures is strict for
$W$ and for $F$:
$$f(W_nH)=f(H)\cap W_nK,\qquad f(F^pH_{\mathbb C})=f(H_{\mathbb C})\cap F^pK_{\mathbb C}$$
for all $n,p$. Its kernel, image and cokernel, with the induced or quotient
filtrations, are mixed Hodge structures; the functor $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n$ is
exact; and a morphism from a structure of weights at least $n$ (that is
$W_{n-1}H=0$) to a structure of weights at most $n$ (that is $W_nK=K$) has
pure image of weight $n$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. A **cochain complex in $\mathcal A$**
is a family of objects $(C^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ together with morphisms
$$d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$$
such that
$$d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$$
for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

This page uses the reindexing convention that a cochain complex $C^\bullet$ may
also be read as the chain complex with $(C^\sharp)_n:=C^{-n}$ and
$d^\sharp_n:=d^{-n}$, so that lower and upper indices differ only by the sign
of the grading.

A **rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex** consists of

(a) a bounded-below cochain complex $K_{\mathbb Q}$ of $\mathbb Q$-vector
spaces with an increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes, finite on each
cochain group;

(b) a cochain complex $K_{\mathbb C}$ of $\mathbb C$-vector spaces with an
increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes and a decreasing filtration $F$ by
subcomplexes, again finite on each cochain group;

(c) a morphism of complexes
$\alpha\colon K_{\mathbb Q}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to K_{\mathbb C}$
compatible with the weight filtrations, such that for every $w$ the induced map
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_w\alpha$ is a quasi-isomorphism,

subject to the following axiom: for every integer $w$ the weight-graded
complex $\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK$ has finite-dimensional cohomology, its
differential (induced by $d_K$) is strict for the induced filtration $F$, and
for every $r$ the induced filtration $F$ on
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, together with the induced rational
comparison
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb Q})\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to
H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, is a pure Hodge structure of weight
$r+w$ ([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]).

Here a cochain complex is a complex in the sense of
[[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], a filtration by subcomplexes is
a filtered complex in the sense of [[def-filtered-chain-complex]], a morphism
compatible with the weight filtrations is a filtered chain map in the sense of
[[def-filtered-chain-map]], quasi-isomorphism means
[[def-quasi-isomorphism]], and finiteness on a cochain group $K^n$ means
$W_aK^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $a$ and $W_aK^n=K^n$ for all

A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Complexification and conjugation.** Complex scalars act by
$c(h\otimes z)=h\otimes cz$; this respects the rational balancing relations.
A finite rational basis of $H$ identifies $H_{\mathbb C}$ with the corresponding
finite-dimensional coordinate space over $\mathbb C$. The
$\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of

$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the weight sum is taken over $\mathbb Q$ and the Hodge sum over
$\mathbb C$, using $(H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}K)_{\mathbb C}\cong

$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

over $\mathbb C$ only.

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Complexification and conjugation.** Complex scalars act by
$c(h\otimes z)=h\otimes cz$; this respects the rational balancing relations.
A finite rational basis of $H$ identifies $H_{\mathbb C}$ with the corresponding
finite-dimensional coordinate space over $\mathbb C$. The
$\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every

cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight

$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

where the weight sum is taken over $\mathbb Q$ and the Hodge sum over
$\mathbb C$, using $(H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}K)_{\mathbb C}\cong
H_{\mathbb C}\otimes_{\mathbb C}K_{\mathbb C}$; the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

On $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$ the induced $F$ has $F^0=0$ and $F^{-1}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$, since $F^0\cap W_{-2}=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)\cap\mathbb C e_1=0$; the conjugate filtration satisfies $\bar F^{-1}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$ and $\bar F^0=0$ for the same reason, so the pieces are $H^{-1,-1}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$ and nothing else, and $H^{-1,-1}$ is spanned by the image of $e_1$, which is rational. On $\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$ the image of $F^0\cap W_0=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)$ is all of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$ because $e_0+ie_1\mapsto e_0\ne0$, and $F^1=0$; the conjugate $\bar F^0=\sigma(F^0)=\mathbb C(e_0-ie_1)$ likewise has image all of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$, so the pieces are $H^{0,0}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$ and nothing else. Both graded pieces are therefore $n$-opposed, with the rational structure of $e_1$ and $e_0$ respectively, so $(H,W,F)$ is a rational mixed Hodge structure; its graded pieces are $\mathbb Q(1)$ and $\mathbb Q(0)$ in the convention [F2].

Let $\iota\colon\mathbb Q(1)\to H$ be the rational inclusion $1\mapsto e_1$, whose complexification is $\mathbb C\to H_{\mathbb C}$ and let $\pi\colon H\to\mathbb Q(0)$ be the $\mathbb Q$-linear map $e_0\mapsto1$, $e_1\mapsto0$. Both preserve the filtrations: $\iota$ sends the weight-$(-2)$ structure into $W_{-2}H=\mathbb Q e_1$ and $F^{-1}\mathbb Q(1)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ into $F^{-1}H_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$, while $F^0\mathbb Q(1)_{\mathbb C}=0$; and $\pi$ satisfies $\pi(W_{-1}H)=0=W_{-1}\mathbb Q(0)$ and $\pi(W_0H)=\mathbb Q(0)=W_0\mathbb Q(0)$, $\pi(F^0H_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\mathbb C=F^0\mathbb Q(0)_{\mathbb C}$ and $\pi(F^1H_{\mathbb C})=0$. Hence $0\to\mathbb Q(1)\xrightarrow{\iota}H\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathbb Q(0)\to0$ is a short exact sequence of rational mixed Hodge structures, with $\ker\pi=\mathbb Q e_1$.

Every $\mathbb Q$-linear section $s$ of $\pi$ satisfies $s(1)=e_0+q e_1$ with $q\in\mathbb Q$, because $\pi(e_0+q e_1)=1$ and $\pi(e_1)=0$. If $s$ were a morphism of mixed Hodge structures, it would satisfy $s_{\mathbb C}(F^0\mathbb Q(0)_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^0H_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)$; since $F^0\mathbb Q(0)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ and $s_{\mathbb C}(1)=e_0+qe_1$, there would be $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $e_0+qe_1=\lambda(e_0+ie_1)$. Comparing the coefficients of $e_0$ and $e_1$ in the basis $(e_0,e_1)$ gives $\lambda=1$ and $q=i$, which is impossible for $q\in\mathbb Q$. The obstruction is visible directly in the $(0,0)$-direction: $F^0H_{\mathbb C}\cap\bar F^0H_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)\cap\mathbb C(e_0-ie_1)=0$, while a rational section must send $1$ into a rational vector of $F^0$, which is then also fixed by conjugation and hence would have to lie in this zero intersection.
